body: I think this check needs to be trivially destructible *and* constructable since we are moving.

I don't think this is safe, I think we need to do a semantic move here, we can't rely on a memmove as we don't know if say, the elements have pointers to themselves. We have to call ctors and dtors here, *or* use an std::move.

I don't think so. No construction is taking place, so trivial constructability is unnecessary. In the case of trivial destructability, but nontrivial constructability:
- all objects are relocated
- the array is shrunk
    - the final object is trivially destructible, so the memory is merely reinterpreted without any destructor calls

You are correct; this will fail for objects that have pointers to themselves. I have linked in my PR [a list](https://open-std.org/JTC1/SC22/WG21/docs/papers/2020/p1144r5.html#non-trivial-samples) of incompatible instances. 

I don't think Godot has any of them. But if we _really_ want to be safe, I'm OK with closing this PR and re-implementing it to just use move semantics.

I see now that you acknowledge this in the document you linked. However I don't think we need to invent new footguns in core/ we need a way to catch this and make it a compiler error if we want to have a happy path for relocatable classes. Maybe even just add a Godot specific type trait.
That seems reasonable. I'll make this PR a draft until we have a `is_trivially_relocatable`-like type trait. Until then, I will optimize this function by using move semantics in another PR.
why move it before destructing it ? why not just call the destructor directly on it, and after just move every element in the tail one index down.
I wish I could do it, but `resize()` calls the destructor for all removed elements. I opened #100474 with the ulterior motive to have access to a non-destructor calling resize function :)
That problem would be better covered under nontrivial relocatability, as discussed below, so I'm closing this one.
